items.title: security(identity): keep passwords and JWTs out of authentication logs

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: security-adjacent
labels.description: Touches security-sensitive surface; extra care and review

labels.name: app/identity
labels.description: Package/app: identity (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

items.body:
## Problem

Authentication paths currently write credential material to application logs:

- `pkgs/identity/cmd/ssh/ssh.go:210-216` logs submitted SSH passwords and keyboard-interactive responses; `Connect` logs the plaintext password and its derived hash at lines 787 and 796-812.
- `pkgs/identity/web/web.go:135` registers `/set-cookie`; its handler reads a JWT at lines 401-410 and logs the token, parsed token, connection, and token/cookie again at lines 408, 416, 430, and 441.

Anyone with access to the service journal or log collection can recover credentials or replay tokens from these entries. Keep useful authentication observability, but emit only non-secret metadata.

## Required behavior

Never log plaintext passwords, password-derived authentication material, JWTs/cookies, or structured objects that contain them. Replace them with safe metadata such as authentication method, outcome, and non-sensitive identifiers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Capture logs while exercising SSH password auth, keyboard-interactive auth, and `/set-cookie` with a valid JWT; assert each injected sentinel credential is absent from all emitted log records.
- Retain useful non-secret outcome/method logs for success and failure paths.
- Include invalid-token/error-path coverage so errors do not echo the submitted credential.

items.title: design: secrets plane — delta refresh, broker peer sync, dual-store puts
items.body:
# Design: secrets plane — delta refresh, broker peer sync, dual-store puts

Direction: Drew, 2026-11-23 ~19:12 CST. Extends #13893 (cold-refresh batching + client fallback bound) and #13894 (broker performance under load). Where this design and #13893's batching-only proposal overlap, **this design supersedes the batching-only framing**: the one-call list becomes the full-refresh mechanism *inside* a delta-first design, not the end state. #13893's client-wait bound survives unchanged (Slice 1 below). #13894 remains the performance-tracking issue; this design addresses its cold-refresh row and part of the client pile-up cause.

Related, not duplicated: #10358 (secrets scoping — prefix / vault / store selection decides *which* store and namespace a name resolves to; this design decides *how* brokers and stores stay in sync), #9158 (canonical secrets model, provider adapters & custody policy), #13081 (heal cadence starving refresh — fixed), #5504 (partial refresh evicting cached secrets — its failure mode is a correctness constraint on Slice 2).

## 1. Problem and evidence

The sandbox secrets broker refreshes by shelling out to `bws secret get <id>` **once per secret** — 242 spawns, ~160–220s cold (measured 2026-11-23, #13893). Refresh runs at startup and every 900s. During that window the broker is present-but-not-serving, and clients hang instead of falling back (>120s observed, #13893), so every sandbox restart wedges every secrets consumer for minutes. The estate has two brokers (sandbox + laptop) holding the same set with no way to learn from each other: if the laptop broker refreshed a minute ago, the sandbox broker still pays the full upstream cost. Writes are worse: `fleet secrets` is read-only today (verified, §3), so a new secret is minted out-of-band in one store and propagates only when a refresh happens to notice it (#6275's read-through gap is the same shape).

## 2. Goals and non-goals

**Goals**

1. A broker restart reaches `serving` in seconds in the normal case (peer up), and in one upstream list call in the worst case (peer down, no cache).
2. Refresh cost tracks *change*, not set size: pull only secrets whose revision moved since the last refresh.
3. Brokers prove sync with a set hash; equal hashes mean synced, full stop.
4. `fleet secrets` gains a write path (`put`) and explicit cache controls (`refresh`, `--upstream`, `--no-cache`), with puts propagated so no peer or store has to re-fetch to converge.
5. Both stores (Bitwarden Secrets + 1Password) are kept in sync by construction, with one designated primary so sync direction is never ambiguous.

**Non-goals**

- Namespaces / per-device store selection — that is #10358; v1 syncs the whole set, per Drew's explicit simplification ("for broker-to-broker, it might just be simpler to just send everything it has from one location to the other… we can pull that back at that point").
- Replacing either store, or embedding them in the fleet binary — filed as separate future-work to-dos, cross-linked below.
- A new trust root or enrollment system — peer trust is the fleet enrollment/broker trust already in place.

## 3. Verified premises

Verified by the filing lane 2026-11-24; anything not verified live is marked.

- **`fleet secrets` today has exactly two verbs, `get` and `list`, and is read-only** — verified from the installed binary's help (`Commands: get, list`). `refresh` and `put` are new surface.
- **`bws secret list <project>` returns the whole set in one call, including values and a per-secret `revisionDate`** — verified live against the estate's Bitwarden project (bws 2.1.0): 244 secrets, fields `creationDate, id, key, note, organizationId, projectId, revisionDate, value` (count and field names only were inspected; no values). So both batching and delta-by-`revisionDate` are supported by the CLI *today*; the broker simply doesn't use the list call.
- **bws write verbs exist** (`bws secret create / edit / delete`) — verified from CLI surface and existing estate scripts.
- **1Password CLI (`op` 2.41.0) is installed** in the sandbox recovery bin and on the laptop — verified. `op item create` / `op item edit` exist (help verified). `op service-account ratelimit` exists (help verified) — service-account rate limits are a real, queryable constraint, not a theoretical one.
- **NOT live-verified:** `op item list --format json` field shape. Documented behaviour is that items carry `created_at` / `updated_at`, and list returns metadata (values need a per-item `op item get`). The laptop's `op` has no account configured in a plain SSH shell ("No accounts configured for use with 1Password CLI"), so this lane did not read a live item. Slice 5 includes a capability spike to verify before the mirror-write path is built on it.
- **Peer channel exists**: the tiered broker shape (local → laptop → in-process) and its tokens (by name: `fleet.secrets-broker-token`, `fleet.queue-broker-token`, `fleet.laptop-agent-token`) are live; sandbox↔laptop traffic rides the tailnet (DERP-relayed at 490–873ms RTT per #13894, still WireGuard-encrypted end to end).

## 4. Alternatives considered

**A. Batching only (#13893 as filed).** One `bws secret list` per refresh replaces 242 gets. Cold refresh drops from ~3–4 min to seconds. Honest tradeoff: refresh cost still scales with set size, brokers still can't learn from each other, no write path, no sync proof. Necessary but not sufficient — absorbed as the full-refresh mechanism in the chosen shape.

**B. Delta refresh from the upstream store only (no peer sync).** Refresh = list, filter `revisionDate > watermark`, apply changes. Cheapest correct refresh, but a restarted sandbox broker with an empty cache still needs a full set from upstream, and two brokers can hold different sets between refreshes with no way to know. Rejected as the end state; it is the upstream half of the chosen shape.

**C. Full-set broker-to-broker transfer on every sync.** Drew's allowed v1 simplification taken literally for *every* cycle: brokers just send each other everything. Simple and obviously correct; at ~244 small secrets the payload is trivial today. Tradeoff: it re-sends everything forever and gives no cheap "are we synced?" answer. The chosen shape keeps full-set transfer as the v1 *peer payload* but gates it behind the set hash, so the common case is one hash comparison and transfers happen only on real divergence.

**D. Store-level replication only (no broker protocol).** Brokers stay dumb caches; Bitwarden and 1Password are synced by a separate replicator. Rejected: it does nothing for the restart wedge (the actual incident), and broker-to-broker is where the latency pain lives.

## 5. Chosen approach

### 5.1 Delta refresh (upstream leg)

Each broker keeps a durable watermark: the start time of its last successful refresh, minus a small skew overlap (Drew's "from maybe just before the last refresh started"). A refresh is one `bws secret list` call; entries with `revisionDate` after the watermark are applied, ids absent from the list are deleted locally, everything else is untouched. The list call carries values, so a delta refresh and a full refresh are the same call with different apply rules — there is no per-secret fetch path left. A failed or partial list applies **nothing** (the #5504 lesson: a partial refresh must never evict).

### 5.2 Broker-to-broker peer sync

On startup and on each refresh tick, a broker asks its trusted peer for `{set_hash, last_upstream_refresh_at, count}`:

- Hashes equal → synced; done. This is the steady state and costs one round trip.
- Peer refreshed from upstream more recently than local, hashes differ → pull the peer's full set (v1 payload = everything, per Drew's simplification) and adopt it, recording the peer as the source and the peer's watermark as the local watermark.
- Peer down or stale → fall back to the upstream delta/full refresh (§5.1).

Consequence, as Drew specified: a sandbox broker needs a full upstream refresh **only if the laptop is down AND it restarted with no cache**. Namespaces and selective pull-back are deferred until requirements actually diverge.

### 5.3 Set hash

The sync proof is a hash over the whole set: sort by name, hash each `(name, value)` pair, combine. Because a bare hash of a low-entropy value is guessable offline, pair hashes are **keyed** (HMAC with the peer token) and the set hash is exchanged only between authenticated brokers, never logged in full (truncated in logs) and never published. Equal keyed hashes from two brokers that share the peer key prove the sets are identical without either side sending values.

### 5.4 Client surface

- `fleet secrets get <name>` — unchanged default path (local broker → laptop → in-process).
- `fleet secrets get <name> --upstream` — resolve from the upstream peer/store, bypassing the local cache.
- `fleet secrets get <name> --no-cache` — bypass all broker caches; straight to the primary store.
- `fleet secrets refresh` — force the local broker through §5.2/§5.1 now instead of at the next tick; reports which leg served it (peer / upstream-delta / upstream-full) and the resulting set hash.
- `fleet secrets put <name>` — new; §5.5. (Value via stdin/prompt, never argv, so it stays out of shell history and process lists.)
- The #13893 client bound rides along: a non-serving local broker is a cache miss within ~2–5s, never a hang.

### 5.5 Put semantics (chosen default)

**Default: the put is written by the node that receives it to the primary store first; that write is the commit point. The writer then pushes the value directly to its peer broker and writes the mirror store; the peer never re-fetches.** Drew offered both shapes (send-upstream-and-let-upstream-write, or write-and-push); write-first-then-push is chosen because (a) the primary store is the source of truth, so the commit must land there before any cache holds the value — otherwise a crash between push and store-write leaves caches holding a secret the truth doesn't have; (b) a node holding only one store still works: it sends the put upstream to the laptop (which always has both), and the laptop performs the dual write — that is the send-upstream shape, kept exactly where it's needed, as the escalation path rather than the default. Mirror-store or peer-push failure after the primary commit does not fail the put; it queues a reconcile (§5.6) and the put reports `committed, propagation pending`.

### 5.6 Dual-store sync and the primary designation

**Recommendation: Bitwarden Secrets is the primary; 1Password is the fallback/mirror.** Drew's initial lean was 1Password primary "if that helps", with the reverse explicitly acceptable if better supported. The evidence supports the reverse:

- The entire running broker stack already authenticates to Bitwarden with machine access tokens, headless, today. 1Password on the laptop has no account configured outside its desktop/service-account setup (§3).
- Bitwarden's one list call returns values *and* `revisionDate` — it is the only store that can serve as the delta source. 1Password's list returns metadata only; a full pull is one call per item.
- 1Password service accounts carry rate limits (the CLI ships a `ratelimit` verb to inspect them); a chatty sync loop against 1Password as primary would spend that budget on bookkeeping. As mirror, it receives one write per put — well inside any limit.
- 1Password's strength in this estate is human-side custody and escrow (the IdP CA material is already escrowed there). As mirror/fallback it keeps that role: if Bitwarden is down, brokers serve from cache and 1Password is the human recovery path; reads can fall back to it, writes queue until the primary returns (or Drew rules an emergency promotion).

Sync direction is therefore never ambiguous: primary → mirror, primary → brokers, broker → broker (§5.2). A periodic reconcile compares the primary's set hash against each broker's and (via item metadata) the mirror's, and repairs drift from the primary, logging names only. The only bootstrap case where a node lacks both stores is a node with just the Bitwarden CLI: it uses the canonical Bitwarden path — acquire its access token via the existing bootstrap route (the token is itself a vaulted secret, fetched by name) — and from then on it is a primary-capable node. Per Drew: the only time a node doesn't bootstrap to having both stores reachable is if the canonical path doesn't have the secret or the CLI isn't installed.

## 6. Security analysis

- **Peer trust**: broker-to-broker sync introduces no new trust. Peers authenticate with the existing broker tokens under the existing fleet enrollment; a non-enrolled party cannot request a set, a hash, or a push. Put (§5.5) requires the same enrollment-grade auth as other broker admin surface — it is a write into the estate's secret store and is treated that way.
- **Values in transit**: values move only on (a) the existing broker channel over the tailnet (WireGuard-encrypted; DERP relays see ciphertext, #13894), and (b) broker↔store TLS. No new plaintext path is created. Full-set peer transfer (v1) widens *how much* value material crosses the peer channel per sync, which is why it is gated behind hash divergence instead of running every tick.
- **Hash leakage**: pair hashes are keyed (§5.3) so a leaked set hash does not enable offline guessing of low-entropy values; hashes are truncated in logs.
- **Logging**: names, counts, timings, truncated hashes, and the serving leg — never values, never full hashes, never tokens. Put audit records name + actor + timestamp only.
- **Deletion**: a delete in the primary propagates as a set-diff deletion (§5.1/§5.2); peer adoption is wholesale-set replacement from the more-recently-refreshed side, so a deleted secret cannot be resurrected by a stale peer — the peer's older watermark loses by rule.

## 7. Build slices (dependency-ordered)

**S1 — Client bound + one-call refresh (the surviving #13893 fixes).** Broker refresh uses one `bws secret list`; clients fall through a non-serving local broker within ~2–5s. *Acceptance:* cold refresh measured in seconds on the live set; a `fleet secrets get` issued during a refresh returns from the laptop tier or errors promptly, never hangs >5s; #13893 closes on this slice's evidence.

**S2 — Delta refresh + watermark.** Durable watermark with skew overlap; apply-only-changed; deletion by id-set diff; partial list applies nothing. *Acceptance:* with exactly one secret changed upstream, refresh applies one entry (log shows names/counts) and the set hash moves; with none changed, refresh is a no-op beyond the list call; a killed mid-refresh broker restarts into the pre-refresh set (no eviction, #5504 regression test).

**S3 — Set hash + peer status.** Keyed set hash (§5.3); brokers expose `{set_hash, last_upstream_refresh_at, count}` to authenticated peers. *Acceptance:* two brokers holding the same set report equal hashes; changing one value on one side flips only that side's hash; unauthenticated hash requests are refused.

**S4 — Peer pull sync.** §5.2 logic on startup and tick; full-set peer payload; upstream fallback. *Acceptance:* sandbox broker cold start with the laptop peer up reaches `serving` with **zero** bws invocations (proven by bws-call logging); cold start with the peer down still reaches `serving` via upstream; a secret changed on the laptop converges to the sandbox on the next tick without either side calling upstream.

**S5 — Client surface: `refresh`, `get --upstream/--no-cache`, `put`.** §5.4/§5.5 semantics, including the one-store-node escalation to the laptop for dual write. Includes the 1Password capability spike (verify §3's unverified premise) before the mirror write is built. *Acceptance:* a put from the sandbox is readable from the laptop broker and present in both stores without waiting for a refresh tick; a put from a Bitwarden-only node lands in both stores via the laptop; `refresh` reports its serving leg; put audit log contains the name and actor and no value.

**S6 — Reconcile + drift repair.** Periodic primary↔broker↔mirror hash comparison; repair from primary; alert on persistent drift. *Acceptance:* a hand-edited mirror entry is detected and restored on the next reconcile, logged by name only; a hand-edited broker cache entry is likewise repaired from the primary; two consecutive failed reconciles raise an alert through the existing PM path.

## 8. Rollout and rollback

Roll out per slice, laptop broker first, sandbox second (the laptop is the estate's always-has-both node and the natural first peer). S1–S2 are broker-internal and roll back by binary revert to the previous published fleet build. S3–S4 add peer verbs behind a config flag defaulting to off until both sides run the new build; disabling the flag returns both brokers to independent upstream refresh (today's behaviour). S5's `put` ships dark (verb present, disabled by config) until S6's reconcile is live, so no write path exists before drift repair does. The stores themselves are never migrated — Bitwarden already holds the set; 1Password mirror population is a one-time copy *from* the primary, verified by hash before S5 enables mirror writes.

## 9. Verification plan

- **Timed cold-start, peer up:** restart the sandbox broker with an empty cache; measure time to `serving`; assert zero bws calls (S4).
- **Timed cold-start, peer down:** stop the laptop broker, restart the sandbox broker empty; it must still reach `serving` via upstream — the one case Drew named where a full upstream refresh is expected — and the elapsed time is recorded against the S1 baseline (one list call, seconds, vs today's ~160–220s).
- **Hash proof:** force a one-value divergence; hashes differ; run sync; hashes equal; sets byte-identical by name+value comparison inside the test harness (values never printed).
- **Put propagation:** put from each node class (dual-store laptop, Bitwarden-only sandbox); verify presence in both stores and both brokers, and timing.
- **Drift drill:** hand-edit the mirror and a broker cache; reconcile repairs both, logs names only.
- **Log audit:** grep all new log paths for a canary value planted via put; it must appear nowhere.

## 10. Open questions (named deciders)

1. **Primary designation** — this design recommends Bitwarden primary / 1Password mirror (§5.6) against Drew's initial lean, on the evidence in §3. **Decider: Drew** (ratify or reverse; the design's mechanics are unchanged if reversed, but the delta source moves and S2/S5 get harder — §5.6 says why).
2. **Put availability** — should `put` work from any enrolled node at S5, or laptop-only until S6 proves reconcile? **Decider: Drew** (security posture call).
3. **Peer protocol home** — extend the secrets broker's own HTTP surface, or carry sync on the queue-broker channel? **Decider: fleet design owner (Archer)**, settled at S3 from the existing broker code, not by preference.
4. **1Password write identity** — service account vs desktop-integration session for the mirror write. **Decider: Archer**, after the S5 capability spike (the laptop CLI currently has no configured account in a plain shell).
5. **Token-generation command name** for the `fleet init` bootstrap to-do (companion issue) — Drew left the name undecided ("I don't know, `fleet generate a net`" was thinking aloud). **Decider: Drew**, when that to-do is picked up.

## 11. Companion to-dos (filed alongside, future work)

- **Embed both stores in the fleet binary** — a configurable feature embedding 1Password + Bitwarden Secrets access directly into `fleet`, so a node downloads one binary and has everything it needs. (Issue link added in a comment below.)
- **`fleet init` bootstrap command** — the one-time-token bootstrap (token redeemed at a generic URL) as a fleet command, plus a token-generation command that talks to the Cloudflare worker and returns a one-time token a service can hand to a new server. (Issue link added in a comment below.)

*Filed by the SECRETS-PLANE-DESIGN lane, 2026-11-24. Secrets are referenced by name only throughout; no values appear in this issue.*

items.body:
# Fleet CA, credentials & secrets — v0.3 design mill (Summit build-out)

**Program epic.** Design-mill run ordered by Drew 2026-11-12 19:28 CST: run the Fleet v0.3 credentials/secrets/CA package through the design mill — preserve every requirement, break it into reviewed component designs, and turn each design into linked, testable implementation issues. A completed design is NOT a completed implementation epic; implementation children stay open until their own acceptance gates pass.

**Intrinsic urgency: 450 (High)** — ahead of normal actionable work (PM charter bands). Dispatch directive: direct Summit session, launched and verified by the orchestrator (this issue's comments carry the launch receipt).

## Authoritative sources (read as ONE intake; precedence: Drew's current instructions → dated addendum refinements → v0.3 spec baseline → decision review proposals → historical inputs)

1. **Muse handoff — Fleet CA, Credentials & Secrets** (Google Doc, modified 2026-11-12): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yeSWQvMIer92zQ4lj99TsTH2oXZem0WfH-WMYKYJpJ0
2. **Fleet v0.3 complete package** (`fleet_architecture_v0_3_complete.zip`, SHA-256 `d853a2bacf391856a863c292b21f5a224352a6681dd81fe55c422040b1fb5644`, internal SHA256SUMS all verified at intake): the governing 50-section spec (§§0–49 + Appendix A), `SECRETS_BACKEND_RESEARCH_2026-11-06.md`, `DECISION_REVIEW_AND_NEXT_STEPS.md`, `fleet_agent_handoff_prompt_v0_3.md`, `source_input_3_architectural_perspective.txt`. Drive: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cdmoblf8yQM2NuXsR2i90N45dABU1EPo/view
3. **Secrets addendum** (architecture/performance/infrastructure follow-up, refines the package): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QkQMPYGEHbjdyMBdrcSdo4i2GKxlJYK2S3PDrvCRfVw/edit
4. **Summit coordinator handoff** (execution contract for this run): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AKDACXObRcUwmJIeCfLaGv6bxcWC00e3rYjOztk4qiY/edit
5. Companion PM charter (shared queue/dispatch conventions ONLY — the CA epic stays separate from PM implementation): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_DQwNbuRmJnITDKKJJ7A3Q0FJa-q2rkzWlz-4PyA_iw/edit

All sources are merged into the repo design directory (see the docs PR linked in comments) and staged on the laptop at `~/.local/share/fleet/intake/fleet-ca-v03-20261112/` (zip hash re-verified after transfer). Repo pinned at intake: `6a7843cae59878e10071f27440b93489053dbc68` (2026-11-12).

## Binding constraints (Drew)

- **ML-DSA-44 is the baseline signature scheme** for the CA design.
- **The Merkle-tree experiment (Cloudflare MTC) is OPTIONAL** — a separate, non-blocking controlled-stack research track; never a v1 dependency. (Handoff doc carries the full MTC analysis: inclusion proofs vs whole certs, landmark/cosigner provisioning, PQ-only separation, byte/CPU/latency comparison against the shortest conventional ML-DSA chain.)

## Scope (from the handoff doc — the CA/credentials workstream, NOT the PM-stack redesign)

Unified secret records + BWS/op/bw adapters (three DIFFERENT provider products — never conflated); daily three-way reconciliation with recoverable `zz.delete` history and false-delete prevention; audit/event journal + provider performance benchmarks; fnox library evaluation (near-term priority); SOPS/age/NixOS integration; password, SSH and iroh generation; reusable Rust APIs + the existing Fleet multicall CLI (no competing tool); PKI root/issuer/leaf lifecycle, publication, packaging, client trust and verification; nonblocking OpenBao/federation/infrastructure research.

**Reference PKI (spec controls):** four independent roots (Ed25519, P-256, RSA, ML-DSA-44), nine asymmetric root cross-certificates (ML-DSA root never signs classical roots by default), Base + Internal Web issuer sets with independent A/B partitions and eligible direct issuer cross-signatures — **20 CA key pairs / 65 CA certificate variants before leaves**. Reference expiries: roots `2050-07-07T12:00:00Z`, both issuer sets `2032-07-07T12:00:00Z` (distinct from the normal 20y/5y/90d defaults). RSA-2048 is a policy-gated compatibility option, not the default long-lived root. Root signing always requires an explicitly authorized signer source — never silently discover/exercise root keys.

**Root custody (addendum refinement):** initial roots escrowed to exactly three approved destinations — encrypted laptop storage, the authorized BWS project, the authorized 1Password vault — with integrity checks and tested restoration; NOT auto-extended to every future provider. R2 is a researched additional destination, not automatic authorization. Offline/hardware root signing is the future path; three OpenBao containers on one host are a lab, not three failure domains.

## V1 — what exists today (intake census; the Summit verifies and deepens)

- `fleet` multicall (laptop build, source rev `743966553e`) domains: queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, secrets, gh, search, laptop-agent. **No `cert`/`pki` or `generate` domain exists yet.**
- `fleet secrets get|list`: broker-first resolution with BWS fallback; name-only references; values never printed. The secrets broker is in production (see #6767 for a known broker staleness defect). No `put`, no reconciliation, no 1Password adapter in the CLI yet.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/`: fleet, fleet-config, fleet-dispatch, fleet-proxy, fleet-proxy-proto, fleet-queue, fleet-registry, fleet-search, fleet-secrets.
- No prior Fleet v0.3 / PKI / ML-DSA / fnox / zz.delete program issues exist (searched at intake) — this epic and its domain starters are the canonical home. The earlier submission was cancelled per the handoff; nothing was launched from it.

## Safety gates (hard)

Design and synthetic proof only in this program phase. **No production CA generation or signing, no root escrow/export, no live vault writes or reconciliation, no credential rotation, no DNS/trust changes, no live service deployment** is authorized by this handoff. Synthetic fixtures must never be confused with production credentials. Design, synthetic proof, code implementation, and production rollout are separately statused.

## Build-out (Summit owns; design-mill pattern)

Statement inventory (every requirement in the spec + addendum + handoffs, numbered, zero unmapped) → state-of-the-art expansion per component → versioned designs (V1 = exists today; V2+ layer) → ADRs/threat model → granular implementation/test/research issues with measurable acceptance, source IDs, boundaries, tests, rollback → batched questions recorded on THIS issue with chosen defaults (never stall). Domain starter issues are native sub-issues of this epic; the Summit files the granular children under them.

## Supervision

Orchestrator check-ins on the bound Summit session (status, questions, artifacts vs the statement inventory); stall = one nudge, then replacement, recorded here. Durable monitor: the fleet's session-minder coverage plus the supervision record in this issue's comments.

## P-384 ADR — merge remainder (lane oc-code-03, 2026-11-23)

Refs #13778 — the P-384 root-identity dated design-record PR is open (branch certprog/p384-adr, head da81369e67c005fc4ff1e6922470e9466b98a1f8; two files: the new record folder plus one doc/README.md index line). The evidence record on #9163 (comment 7114665610) states READY TO MERGE. The lane does not merge; Archer merges via the GitHub API from that record. Bridging by cross-signing stays behind the production gate.
